title: Patient Identification, Safety, and Tourniquet Concepts

sections.learningObjectives:
- Verify patient identity with two patient-specific identifiers before any blood collection and escalate any mismatch or uncertainty per office policy.
- Apply standard precautions and bloodborne pathogen safety practices, including PPE selection, hand hygiene, and exposure response, when assisting with collections.
- Explain correct tourniquet use, including placement, tightness, and time limits, and recognize the risks of prolonged or overly tight application.
- Prevent wrong-patient, specimen-quality, and injury errors and escalate concerns to licensed staff rather than acting outside scope.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Checking who a person is before you take a sample is like reading the name tag on a backpack before you hand it back, so the right person gets their own things.

### Question 2

Ask the person to tell you their own name and birthday, like asking someone to say their own lunch code instead of guessing it for them.

### Question 3

A name and a birthday together are like a first name plus a secret code; putting the two together points to exactly one person.

### Question 4

Using a room number to identify someone is like calling a locker 'locker 12' instead of using the owner's name; the locker could belong to anyone.

### Question 5

If a name matches but the birthday does not, that is like two puzzle pieces that almost fit; stop and find the right piece before you glue anything.

### Question 6

Asking an open question is like asking a friend to say their own phone number instead of just saying 'yes' to the number you read out.

### Question 7

If a person cannot say their own name, you check their wristband or papers, the way you would read a label on something that cannot talk.

### Question 8

For a small child, you ask the grown-up to say the child's full name and birthday, then check it against the child's wristband, like matching a name tag to a list.

### Question 9

When two kids have nearly the same name, you check their birthdays too, like looking at two similar boxes and reading the small print to tell them apart.

### Question 10

Just because someone signed in at the front desk does not mean the right person is in the room now, so you check again right before the poke.

### Question 11

If someone will not tell you who they are, you do not take the sample; you stop and ask the person in charge what to do.

### Question 12

A medical record number is like a library card number that belongs to just one person, so it helps pick the right person out of a crowd.

### Question 13

You compare what the person says to the paper or screen that lists the test, the way a cashier matches your name to the order you placed.

### Question 14

If you accidentally label a test with the wrong person's name, a doctor might treat the wrong person for something they do not have.

### Question 15

If a person cannot hear well, you write the question down or show it on a screen so they can tell you their own name and birthday.

### Question 16

If someone speaks another language, you bring in someone who can translate so they can tell you their own name and birthday correctly.

### Question 17

When someone is asleep or unconscious, you read their wristband and check it against the paper, like checking a luggage tag.

### Question 18

If the wristband is missing, you stop and get a new one first, like getting a fresh name tag before a field trip.

### Question 19

Two name tags with different birthdays is like two labels on one package; you stop and get help instead of guessing.

### Question 20

Even when you are in a hurry, you still check the name and birthday, like a crossing guard who always looks both ways no matter how late it is.

### Question 21

You match the official name on the paper, then call the person by the name they like, the way a school roll uses a legal name but a teacher uses a nickname.

### Question 22

When someone tells you an order out loud, you repeat it back, like repeating a pizza order so the kitchen gets it right.

### Question 23

If you are not sure who someone is, you ask for help, even if you are in a rush, because guessing is how mix-ups happen.

### Question 24

The person doing the collecting is the one who double-checks the name, like the person handing out report cards checks each name.

### Question 25

Writing down how you checked the name is like saving the receipt, so later you can show you did the check.

### Question 26

A birthday is like a second password that does not change, helping tell apart two people with the same name.

### Question 27

You treat every sample as if it might carry germs, the way you handle raw eggs carefully even when they look clean.

### Question 28

You put on gloves when you might touch blood, like wearing an apron when you might get splattered.

### Question 29

If blood might spray, you add a face shield and a cover-up, like wearing goggles and a smock when something might splatter.

### Question 30

Even after taking off gloves you wash your hands, like washing your hands after taking off dish gloves, because the outside touched germs.

### Question 31

The big three germs that can pass through blood are hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, so workers protect against those.

### Question 32

If blood gets in your eye, you rinse it right away under water, like washing out sand, and then tell the person in charge.

### Question 33

Workers who might touch blood get a free shot to protect them from hepatitis B, like getting a flu shot before flu season.

### Question 34

The exposure control plan is the office's safety rulebook for blood, telling everyone what to do to stay safe and what to do if something goes wrong.

### Question 35

If you get a needle poke, you wash it with soap and water right away and tell someone in charge, like cleaning a scrape and telling a grown-up.

### Question 36

If blood spills, you put on gloves first, then clean it up with the right supplies, like putting on gloves before wiping up a mess.

### Question 37

You do not eat or drink where blood is handled, the same way you would not eat in a chemistry lab.

### Question 38

Once your gloves have touched blood, you keep them off the phone and keyboard, like keeping dirty gardening gloves off the kitchen counter.

### Question 39

You have the person sit or lie down first, like buckling a seatbelt before the car moves, so they cannot fall if they get dizzy.

### Question 40

If someone says they feel dizzy, you stop and help them lie down, like helping a teammate sit before they fall.

### Question 41

If someone turns pale and sweaty and says they feel faint, that is a warning light that they might fall, so you act fast.

### Question 42

If someone is allergic to latex, you use the special non-latex gloves and band, like using a different ingredient for a food allergy.

### Question 43

You use tongs or a dustpan to pick up broken glass, like using a tool to grab something sharp, and put it in the special sharps bin.

### Question 44

A used needle goes straight into the sharps bin right away, like throwing a wrapper in the trash the moment you are done.

### Question 45

When two people share a sharp tool, they set it down on a tray and the other picks it up, like passing scissors by putting them on the table.

### Question 46

You cannot always tell who has germs just by looking, so you treat every sample carefully, like washing produce even when it looks clean.

### Question 47

Even if a friend says it is fine, you still follow the safety rule and wear gloves, like always wearing a seatbelt even for a short trip.

### Question 48

If you do not know the safe way to do something, you stop and ask someone who knows, like asking a teacher before using a new tool.

### Question 49

The tourniquet is like pinching a garden hose gently so the water backs up a little and the hose bulges, making the vein easier to find.

### Question 50

You tighten the band just enough to slow the blood going back, not enough to squeeze the blood coming in, like a gentle squeeze, not a full pinch.

### Question 51

Leaving the band on too long is like holding a pinch too long; the blood pools and the arm starts to complain, so you let go quickly.

### Question 52

You let go of the band before you pull the needle out, like loosening a clamp before removing a plug.

### Question 53

If the band is on too long, the blood gets 'thick' and some numbers read higher than they really are, like measuring syrup instead of water.

### Question 54

Little red dots after a draw can mean the band was squeezed too tight or too long, like a pinch leaving small marks.

### Question 55

If the band is too tight, the arm can go numb and tingly, like a rubber band wrapped too hard around a finger.

### Question 56

You put the band over the sleeve or a small pad, like putting a bandage over a sore spot instead of on it.

### Question 57

A band that touches many people without being cleaned is like sharing a straw, so it gets cleaned or thrown away between people.

### Question 58

For someone allergic to latex, you use the special rubber-free band, like using a different kind of bandage for sensitive skin.

### Question 59

You set up the band so you can let go with one quick pull, like tying a bow that comes undone easily.

### Question 60

If the arm starts to hurt, you let go of the band and rethink, like stopping to loosen a too-tight shoelace.

### Question 61

Between tries, you let go and give the arm a short break, like resting between two tries of a hard task.

### Question 62

For an older person with delicate skin, you squeeze the band very gently and let go quickly, like handling a delicate package with care.

### Question 63

Some arms have a special access or healing area that must not be squeezed, like not pinching an arm that is already hurt, so you use the other arm.

### Question 64

Once the blood is flowing, you let go of the band so the later tubes do not get 'thick' blood, like releasing a hose clamp once water flows.

### Question 65

You never leave a squeeze band on someone and walk away, like never leaving a clamp on and forgetting it.

### Question 66

You do not put the band right where you will poke, like not covering the exact spot you want to reach.

### Question 67

If you can already see the vein clearly, you might not need the squeeze band at all, like not using a flashlight when the sun is out.

### Question 68

If a blood pressure cuff is used as a squeeze band, it is pumped just a little, not all the way, so blood can still flow in.

### Question 69

If the band is ripped, you throw it away and get a fresh one, like replacing a broken shoelace instead of tying the pieces together.

### Question 70

For a hand poke, you put the band a little above the wrist, like putting a hair tie above the wrist, not on the fingers.

### Question 71

The band plumps up the vein so you can feel it better, like filling a balloon a little so you can see its shape.

### Question 72

The band just helps you find the vein; it does not do any of the other safety jobs, like checking the name.

### Question 73

If someone passes out, you take the band off right away and keep them from falling, like catching a friend and loosening anything tight.

### Question 74

For someone who bruises easily, you squeeze the band lightly and let go fast, then press on the spot longer, like being extra gentle with fragile fruit.

### Question 75

Squeezing too hard over and over is like pinching the same spot many times; it leaves a bruise.

### Question 76

The whole point of checking names and being careful is to make sure the right person gets the right answer about their health.

### Question 77

You can work quickly, but you still do every safety check, like a chef who cooks fast but still washes hands and checks the order.

### Question 78

If you almost grabbed the wrong cup but caught yourself, you tell someone so the team can fix what caused the mix-up.

### Question 79

If you cannot find the vein after a couple of tries, you stop and get help instead of poking over and over, like calling for backup instead of guessing.

### Question 80

Pressing on the spot after the needle comes out is like pressing on a small leak to stop it and prevent a bruise.

### Question 81

The assistant helps and follows the rules, and calls a grown-up (a licensed person) when something is beyond what they are allowed to do.

### Question 82

If you are not sure something matches, you stop and ask, like checking with the teacher instead of guessing on a test.

### Question 83

If you realize you took the sample from the wrong person, you stop and tell the person in charge right away, like raising your hand when you make a mistake.

### Question 84

Before you start, you make sure the person is sitting or lying safely and the floor is clear, like clearing toys before running around.

### Question 85

If something goes wrong, you write down exactly what happened, like telling the truth in a report so it can be fixed.

### Question 86

When someone asks what a test result means, the assistant hands the question to the doctor, like a referee calling in an expert.

### Question 87

Following the rules keeps both the patient and the helper safe, like wearing helmets protects both the rider and the person they ride with.
